segments.visible_description: A wide view shows six women working across the room-sized ENIAC cabinets.
segments.narration: In 1945 the Army switches on the thirty-ton ENIAC in Philadelphia to calculate artillery tables.
segments.editorial_purpose: Establish the machine's physical scale and the six women in the room from the start.

segments.visible_description: A closer view shows women tracing and connecting ENIAC cables and switches by hand.
segments.narration: A machine this new has no instructions; somebody must teach it physically, and the Army gives that work to six women.
segments.editorial_purpose: Move from scale to hands-on programming as soon as the narration does.

segments.visible_description: The six programmers work together at ENIAC while a record of the public credit gap appears within the composition.
segments.narration: Jean, Betty, Kay, Marlyn, Ruth and Frances.
segments.editorial_purpose: Give the spoken names a group frame before the detailed programming explanation begins.

segments.visible_description: Women physically rewire ENIAC cable by cable and switch by switch.
segments.narration: With no manual or programming language, they program the machine by hand and work out how to make it follow a plan.
segments.editorial_purpose: Return after the names to the exact physical action the longer technical explanation describes.

segments.visible_description: Comic emphasis card reading ‘The First Programmers.’
segments.narration: They are, quite literally, the first programmers.
segments.editorial_purpose: Reserve the exact title card for the exact claim.

segments.visible_description: The public-credit composition reveals named men while the women who programmed ENIAC remain unnamed beside the machine.
segments.narration: At the press showing the men in the photographs are named; the six women standing at the machine are not.
segments.editorial_purpose: Use the existing credit-reveal event only across the credit-erasure narration it depicts, then match-cut into the fuller rediscovery evidence page.

segments.visible_description: A comic evidence page contrasts the women programming ENIAC, the credited men, and the rediscovered six names under the line ‘It took forty years to learn who they were.’
segments.narration: People assumed the women were models; it took about forty years to learn who they actually were.
segments.editorial_purpose: Make both the false assumption and later rediscovery visible in one exact evidence page.

segments.visible_description: The room-sized ENIAC and its programmers fill the frame again before the historical jump.
segments.narration: That reckoning comes later; for now machines are about to leap ahead and bring a new headache.
segments.editorial_purpose: Return to the machine, after the rediscovery page, to motivate the next technical era rather than inventing a new historical claim.

segments.visible_description: The exact comic time-jump announces ‘Philadelphia, 1952’ over the computer room.
segments.editorial_purpose: Place the truthful time-jump exactly on the spoken date and hand off into the next language sequence.

required_gate: independent six-programmer likeness, names and historical-detail review
independent judgment that credit-reveal and time-jump retimes remain natural
independent p24/p25 and p27/p28 transition review
